page.title: Lesson Overview
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 5 | Lesson 1 | Page 1 of 6

Lesson Overview: Revision from Adult, Peer, and Online Feedback

Lesson Focus

Primary: MLA.CW.REV.01.
Supporting: MLA.CW.COM.02 and MLA.CW.WR.08. Learn to evaluate feedback, protect authorial purpose, revise substantially, and document decisions.

What You Will Learn

  • Separate reader response, diagnosis, suggestion, correction, and preference.
  • Evaluate authority, specificity, evidence, relevance, and risk.
  • Resolve conflicting feedback without surrendering ownership.
  • Use revision evidence to explain what changed and why.

Why This Matters

Creative writing helps you communicate ideas, experiences, and perspectives with purpose. Each lesson strengthens your ability to read like a writer, make deliberate craft choices, revise thoughtfully, and explain how those choices affect a reader. These skills build creative confidence, clear communication, and responsible participation in a writing community.

What You Will Do

  • Learn and apply the lesson vocabulary.
  • Follow step-by-step instruction and study worked examples.
  • Practice through interactive checks and guided application.
  • Complete Independent Work to apply the lesson skills.
  • Complete a separate Checkpoint to demonstrate your understanding.

Lesson Workflow

  1. Complete Pages 1–4 in order.
  2. Complete Page 5 and submit it with your Page 2 vocabulary in Notebook Evidence Submission.
  3. Complete Page 6 and submit it separately in Checkpoint Submission.
  4. Review TOR feedback, correct errors, and resubmit any work scoring below 80%.
  5. Complete the assessment listed after the lesson. A score of at least 80% is required.

page.title: Vocabulary and Definitions
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 5 | Lesson 1 | Page 2 of 6

Vocabulary and Definitions

Notebook Task: Record every core term and its complete meaning in your notebook. Submit these vocabulary notes with your Independent Work as Notebook Evidence. Use the examples to see how each term works in context. Reference glossary terms do not need to be copied.
TermMeaningExample
feedbackInformation about how a reader experiences a draft.A reader reports where tension faded and where curiosity increased.
reader responseA description of a reader’s reaction or understanding.“I became confused when the narrator entered the station” is a reader response.
diagnosisAn explanation of the underlying craft problem.The confusion comes from an unclear time shift, not the setting itself.
suggestionA proposed way to revise.Add a transition before the flashback is a specific suggestion.
criterionA standard used to judge effectiveness.Clarity of cause and effect is one criterion for evaluating the scene.
authorial purposeThe writer’s intended meaning or effect.The authorial purpose is to make the reader distrust the narrator.
triageSorting feedback by urgency, value, and scope.A missing climax receives attention before a single weak adjective.
feedback patternA concern repeated by independent readers.Three readers missing the same motivation signals a feedback pattern.
conflicting feedbackRecommendations pointing toward incompatible revisions.One reader asks for more explanation while another prefers greater ambiguity.
revision hypothesisA testable prediction about how a change will improve the draft.If the clue appears earlier, readers should understand the final decision without added exposition.
change logA record of feedback, decisions, revisions, and results.The log connects each major change to its source and outcome.
source credibilityThe trustworthiness and relevant expertise of a feedback source.A genre-aware peer may offer credible advice about mystery pacing.

Vocabulary in Action

Match each clue to the precise term. Choose Check, study any mismatch, and retry. This practice is ungraded.

Make the Vocabulary Work

Which response is a diagnosis rather than only a suggestion?

A. “Move the explanation to the opening paragraph.”

Not the best choice. This proposes an action, but it does not identify the craft problem the change is meant to solve.

B. “Readers cannot connect the final decision to the conflict because the character’s motivation appears after the climax.”

Best choice. It identifies the underlying problem and explains how placement affects comprehension, providing a basis for a targeted revision.

page.title: Lesson
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 5 | Lesson 1 | Page 3 of 6

Lesson: The Feedback-to-Revision Protocol

Eight-Step Protocol

  1. Restate the writing goal and nonnegotiable purpose.
  2. Record feedback exactly before reacting.
  3. Classify it: response, diagnosis, suggestion, correction, or preference.
  4. Evaluate source credibility and relevant expertise.
  5. Locate textual evidence for the reported problem.
  6. Cluster repeated concerns and resolve conflicts by criterion.
  7. Write a revision hypothesis, test a change, and compare before/after effects.
  8. Accept, adapt, or set aside the advice and document the reason.

Visual Decision Matrix

FeedbackEvidenceGoal fitDecision
“I lost track of time.”two unmarked jumpsclarity requiredaccept problem; adapt solution

Pause and Choose: Diagnose Before Revising

A reader says, “The middle dragged.” Which writer response turns that reaction into a useful revision test?

A. “I will delete the middle because the reader disliked it.”
Weaker choice. The writer treats a response as a complete diagnosis and adopts a solution without finding evidence. The real issue might be repetition, weak stakes, unclear time, or misplaced detail.
B. “I will mark where the goal stalls, test whether repeated explanation slows the pace, and compare a tighter version with the original.”
Stronger choice. This preserves the reader’s valid experience, locates textual evidence, forms a revision hypothesis, and tests an effect before committing to the change.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

Learning Routes

  • Visual: color-code feedback categories and repeated patterns.
  • Auditory: explain the revision hypothesis aloud before editing.
  • Hands-on: sort feedback cards into accept, adapt, test, and set aside.

Pause and Choose: Protect Purpose and Voice

Two readers ask for more explanation, but the piece intentionally uses a child narrator who understands less than the audience. Which decision is best?

A. Clarify the surrounding evidence while preserving the narrator’s limited language and perspective.
Stronger choice. This adapts the feedback to the writing goal. Readers receive stronger orientation, but the revision does not erase the deliberate voice that creates the piece’s dramatic tension.
B. Replace the child’s voice with an adult explanation because repeated feedback must always be accepted exactly.
Weaker choice. Repetition makes the concern worth investigating, not the proposed solution automatically correct. This change would violate the piece’s nonnegotiable purpose.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

Online Feedback Safety

Do not share private identifying information or unpublished work in public spaces without permission. Evaluate anonymity, expertise, evidence, possible bias, platform incentives, and whether advice attempts to imitate another writer or erase your voice.

page.title: Worked Example
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 5 | Lesson 1 | Page 4 of 6

Worked Example: Three Feedback Decisions

Example 1 — Accept the Problem, Adapt the Solution

Peer: “Cut the flashback; it is confusing.” Evidence shows the time shift is unmarked, but the flashback supplies motive. The writer keeps it, adds a sensory trigger and clear return line, then retests. Clarity improves without losing purpose.

Pause and Choose: A or B

Which response shows the strongest use of peer feedback?

A. The writer cuts the flashback immediately because a peer called it confusing.
Weaker response. This treats feedback as a command and sacrifices an important purpose without diagnosing the actual problem.
B. The writer confirms that the unmarked time shift causes confusion, keeps the flashback because it supplies motive, adds a sensory trigger and return line, and then retests clarity.
Stronger response. This response separates the reader’s valid difficulty from the proposed solution, then tests a revision that protects the writer’s purpose.

Retry: Close your first choice and open the other. Compare both explanations before continuing.

Example 2 — Resolve Conflict

Adult reader: “Explain the ending.” Peer: “Keep it ambiguous.” Criterion: readers should understand the choice but debate its consequence. Revision clarifies what the character does while preserving the uncertain result. Both responses identify different parts of the same problem.

Example 3 — Evaluate Online Advice

Anonymous comment: “Make the narrator likable.” It gives no evidence and conflicts with the goal of portraying self-deception. The writer sets aside the preference but tests whether the narrator’s motive is legible. A concrete remembered detail improves comprehension without making the narrator admirable.

Change-Log Model

Feedback → evidence → criterion → decision → before/after change → observed result. A strong log explains reasoning rather than merely listing edits.

Your Turn Before Independent Work

Pause and try: A peer says, “Make the ending happier.” Explain how you would diagnose the reader need before accepting, adapting, or declining the suggestion.

Check your thinking — open after you try
Teacher model: I would ask which evidence made the ending feel unsatisfying and compare that response with my intended effect. I might strengthen resolution without changing the emotional outcome, then test the revision with a new reader.

page.title: Independent Work
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 5 | Lesson 1 | Page 5 of 6

Independent Work: Revision from Adult, Peer, and Online Feedback

Purpose

Evaluate feedback and make revision decisions that strengthen the writer’s purpose without surrendering ownership.

Complete each numbered part in your notebook. Use precise evidence from your own work and the source provided.

Source for Your Work

Draft line: “The room was tense when I entered.” Feedback A: Add a concrete detail that lets readers feel the tension. Feedback B: Change the narrator to third person. Feedback C: The opening needs more energy.

1. Plan Before You Work

DecisionYour Plan
Purpose and intended audienceState each clearly.
Most important craft or communication needName the need and evidence.
Success indicatorDescribe what an effective result will do for a reader.

2. Choose and Explain

Which approach demonstrates stronger decision-making? Record A or B, then explain your choice in 2–3 sentences using a lesson concept.

A. Accept every suggestion because feedback is automatically correct.
B. Compare each suggestion with the purpose, identify the underlying concern, and adopt, adapt, or decline it with a reason.

3. Apply the Lesson

Use a 250–350 word excerpt from your own earlier work or the draft seed above. Create a feedback log for the three comments, label each Adopt, Adapt, or Decline, explain why, and revise the excerpt using the two most useful ideas.

4. Revise with Purpose

Compare one before-and-after passage. Explain exactly how the revision improves clarity, effect, or reader experience.

Before You Submit

  • All four numbered parts are complete.
  • Your work applies the lesson skill to a specific creative product.
  • Your explanation identifies a decision and its effect on readers.
  • Your revision meaningfully improves the work, not only its appearance.

page.title: Checkpoint
page.contents:
Checkpoint: Revision From Adult, Peer, and Online Feedback

Put the lesson together through analysis, decision-making, writing, and purposeful revision.

Purpose

Show that you can understand the lesson concept, apply it in original work, and explain your decisions. Complete every numbered item and submit your responses with your Checkpoint work.

New Source: Three Notes on One Draft

Draft line: “Mina entered the empty gym and felt nervous about the audition.”

Adult feedback: Clarify what Mina may lose if the audition goes badly.
Peer feedback: Let us hear or see the gym instead of naming the emotion.
Online comment: “Make it more exciting!!!”

Actionable feedback identifies a specific problem and suggests a useful direction. Revision changes meaning, structure, development, or effect—not merely surface errors.

Part 1: Analyze the Source

  1. Which two comments are most actionable? Explain what each helps the writer improve.
  2. How should the writer evaluate the online comment before using it? Name one useful question the writer should ask.

Use this response pattern: Make a precise claim, cite the relevant detail, and explain how the detail proves the claim.

Part 2: Choose A or B

3. Which revision approach protects the writer’s purpose while using feedback responsibly?

A. Accept every suggestion so the revised draft pleases all readers.
B. Compare each suggestion with the purpose, audience, and evidence in the draft; adopt, adapt, or decline it for a stated reason.

Record A or B in your submission and explain your choice in 2–3 sentences. The answer is not revealed here because this item is part of your graded written work.

Part 3: Create and Apply

4. Revise the following seed into a 400–500 word scene: “Mina entered the empty gym and felt nervous about the audition.”

  1. Plan: State the scene’s purpose and intended effect.
  2. Opening: Establish setting, stakes, and character goal without naming the emotion directly.
  3. Development: Use sensory detail and action to build tension.
  4. Turning point: Make Mina choose whether and how to begin.
  5. Resolution: Show the immediate consequence.

Then create a feedback log with the three comments above. Label each adopt, adapt, or decline and explain your reasoning. Make at least two substantive revisions.

Plan before drafting: Decide what the audience should understand, how each section will build that understanding, and which details will do the most work.

Part 4: Revise With Purpose

5. Highlight one revision that changes meaning or effect and one edit that corrects a surface issue. Explain the difference.

Do more than correct spelling. Revise organization, meaning, evidence, or craft so the work becomes clearer and more effective.

Before You Submit

  • Every numbered item is complete.
  • Analysis includes specific evidence and reasoning.
  • The creative work follows the required organization and length.
  • The A/B response is recorded and explained.
  • The revision is visible and its purpose is clear.

Mastery Target

A score of 80% or higher demonstrates mastery. Depth, control, and application matter more than unnecessary length.

TOR Help

If you are unsure how to organize your response, choose evidence, or revise meaningfully, contact your Teacher of Record before submitting.
